explanation: When an investment adviser or a related person serves as the qualified custodian (self-custody), Rule 206(4)-2 requires an annual surprise examination by an independent public accountant registered with the PCAOB. The 'surprise' element means the examination date is not pre-announced. This requirement provides an independent check on the assets held, reducing the risk of fraud when the entity holding and managing the assets is not truly independent.
regulatoryBasis: SEC Rule 206(4)-2 (Custody Rule) — surprise examination requirement

stem: Under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, for how long must a registered investment adviser retain most books and records, and where must the records be kept for the first portion of that period?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 3 years total; records may be kept at any offsite storage facility from the beginning.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The retention period for most adviser records is 5 years, not 3 years. The first 2 years require readily accessible storage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 7 years total; records must be kept at the principal office for the first 5 years.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Seven-year retention applies to certain FINRA broker-dealer records; investment adviser records are generally retained for 5 years. The accessible storage requirement is for the first 2 years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 5 years total; records must be kept in an easily accessible place for the first 2 years.
choices.explanation: Correct. SEC Rule 204-2 requires investment advisers to retain most books and records for 5 years from the end of the fiscal year in which the record was created. For the first 2 years of that period, the records must be maintained in an easily accessible place (e.g., at the principal office).

choices.label: D
choices.text: 5 years total; records must be maintained only in paper form and stored in a fire-proof vault.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Rule 204-2 permits records to be maintained electronically, subject to requirements ensuring integrity and accessibility. There is no requirement for paper-only storage or a fire-proof vault.

explanation: SEC Rule 204-2 requires registered investment advisers to maintain and preserve most books and records for 5 years from the end of the fiscal year in which the document was made. The records must be kept in an easily accessible place for the first 2 years of the retention period. Records may be maintained in electronic format subject to specific conditions regarding accuracy, accessibility, and backup.
regulatoryBasis: SEC Rule 204-2 (Books and Records Rule)

stem: An investment adviser holds a significant position in XYZ stock and recommends it to clients without disclosing this ownership interest. Which component of the adviser's fiduciary duty is MOST directly violated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Duty of care, because the adviser failed to conduct adequate research before recommending XYZ.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The duty of care relates to making recommendations based on reasonable investigation and client suitability. The violation here is about the undisclosed conflict of interest — the adviser's personal financial stake in the recommendation — which is the duty of loyalty.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Net capital rule, because the adviser's concentrated position in XYZ may impair financial condition.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The net capital rule applies to broker-dealers' financial condition and liquidity, not to investment advisers' conflicts of interest. This scenario describes a fiduciary duty violation, not a net capital issue.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Brochure delivery rule, because the adviser failed to deliver Form ADV Part 2A before the recommendation.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. While Form ADV should disclose conflicts of interest, the brochure delivery rule governs the timing of document delivery to new clients — it is not the primary rule violated when an adviser makes a conflicted recommendation without disclosure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Duty of loyalty, because the adviser failed to disclose a material conflict of interest that compromises the objectivity of the recommendation.
choices.explanation: Correct. The duty of loyalty requires investment advisers to act in the client's best interest and to disclose (and manage) conflicts of interest. Recommending securities in which the adviser has an undisclosed financial interest is the textbook example of a duty of loyalty violation — the adviser may be motivated by personal gain rather than client benefit.

explanation: Investment advisers owe clients a fiduciary duty comprising two core obligations: (1) duty of loyalty — act in the client's best interest and disclose/manage conflicts; and (2) duty of care — act on the basis of reasonable investigation and in the client's best interest. Recommending securities without disclosing a personal ownership interest is a classic duty of loyalty violation. Section 206 of the Advisers Act makes this conduct fraudulent.
regulatoryBasis: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 Section 206; fiduciary duty of loyalty

stem: Which statement BEST describes the key difference between the fiduciary standard applicable to investment advisers and the Regulation Best Interest (Reg BI) standard applicable to broker-dealers when making recommendations to retail customers?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There is no meaningful difference; both standards require the professional to act in the client's best interest at all times.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. While both standards use 'best interest' language, they differ in important ways. The fiduciary standard is ongoing and relationship-based; Reg BI is transactional (applies at the time of a recommendation) and does not impose a continuous duty.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fiduciary standard imposes an ongoing duty of loyalty and care throughout the advisory relationship, while Reg BI applies at the point of a recommendation and does not prohibit all conflicts of interest — only requires they be disclosed and mitigated.
choices.explanation: Correct. Investment advisers' fiduciary duty is continuous — it applies throughout the relationship and requires acting in the client's best interest at all times, placing client interests above the adviser's own. Reg BI applies at the time of a recommendation and requires disclosure and mitigation (not elimination) of conflicts. A broker-dealer may still retain certain conflicts under Reg BI if they are disclosed and mitigated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reg BI is a higher standard than the fiduciary standard because it applies federal securities law rather than state common law.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The fiduciary standard is broadly considered a higher standard than Reg BI. Reg BI is a significant enhancement over the prior suitability rule but does not reach the full ongoing fiduciary obligations of investment advisers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The fiduciary standard applies only to discretionary accounts, while Reg BI applies to both discretionary and non-discretionary accounts.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The fiduciary standard applies to all investment adviser client relationships regardless of whether the account is discretionary. The fiduciary duty is triggered by the advisory relationship itself, not the type of account.

explanation: Investment advisers are fiduciaries under the Advisers Act, subject to an ongoing, relationship-based duty of loyalty (client interest first, manage conflicts) and duty of care (reasonable investigation, suitable advice). Reg BI (SEC Release IA-5248) requires broker-dealers to act in the retail customer's best interest at the time of a recommendation and to disclose and mitigate conflicts — but unlike the fiduciary standard, it does not require elimination of all conflicts or impose a continuous duty between recommendations.
regulatoryBasis: Investment Advisers Act of 1940 Section 206; SEC Regulation Best Interest (Rule 15l-1)

stem: An investment adviser representative (IAR) is registered in State A, where the advisory firm is based. A client who lives in State A temporarily relocates to State B for 6 months. The IAR continues to service the client remotely. Under NASAA's de minimis exemption, must the IAR register in State B?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes, immediately upon the client relocating to State B.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. NASAA's de minimis rule provides a grace period for IAR registration when an existing client moves to a new state. Immediate registration is not required.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No, because the IAR has no place of business in State B and serves fewer than the de minimis client threshold.
choices.explanation: Correct. NASAA's model rules provide that an IAR does not need to register in a state where the IAR has no place of business if the IAR serves 5 or fewer clients in that state within a 12-month period. Continuing to service an existing client who temporarily moved falls under this de minimis exemption, especially for fewer than 5 clients.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No, because IAR registration is exclusively a federal requirement handled by FINRA.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. IAR registration is a state-level requirement, not federal. IARs of state-registered advisers register with state securities regulators (not FINRA or the SEC) in states where they have a place of business or exceed de minimis client thresholds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes, but the IAR has 90 days after the client relocates to complete the State B registration.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. While there is a grace period concept in some registrations, the de minimis exemption based on client count is the more applicable rule here. Continued service to a single existing client under the de minimis threshold does not require registration, regardless of a 90-day window.

explanation: NASAA's model rules include a de minimis exemption for IARs: an IAR with no place of business in a state need not register there if the IAR has 5 or fewer clients in that state during any 12-month period. Servicing an existing client who temporarily moves to another state typically falls within this exemption. State registration for IARs is required when they have a place of business in the state or exceed the de minimis client threshold.
regulatoryBasis: NASAA Model Rule 412 — de minimis exemption for IARs

stem: An investment adviser's portfolio manager sells shares of ABC Corp from discretionary client accounts on Monday, knowing the firm will release a research report downgrading ABC on Wednesday. A few days later, several clients complain their accounts sold ABC right before it declined. Which prohibited practice does this describe?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excessive trading (churning), because multiple accounts sold ABC in a short period.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Churning involves excessive transactions designed to generate commissions — it is not about the timing of trades relative to proprietary research. The issue here is the advisers exploiting inside information about their own forthcoming research.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Front-running, because the firm traded ahead of its own research report — a material event that would predictably affect the stock price.
choices.explanation: Correct. Front-running in the research context involves trading in clients' (or proprietary) accounts ahead of the firm's own research action — in this case, selling client holdings before a downgrade report is released. This exploits advance knowledge of a material, non-public (within the firm) event. It is a breach of fiduciary duty and a deceptive practice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Unauthorized trading, because the clients did not specifically authorize the sale of ABC on Monday.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. In discretionary accounts, the adviser is authorized to trade without prior client approval for each transaction. The violation here is the improper motivation (using advance knowledge of the research report), not lack of authorization.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Selling away, because the trades were executed outside the firm's normal order management system.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The question does not state the trades were outside the firm's system. Selling away refers to transactions conducted outside the firm's supervision. The described conduct is front-running.

explanation: Using advance knowledge of a firm's own forthcoming research report to trade ahead of that report — thereby profiting or avoiding loss at clients' expense — is a form of front-running. The firm exploits material non-public information (the downgrade) that it itself controls. This violates fiduciary duty, Section 206 of the Advisers Act, and constitutes a deceptive and manipulative practice. Firms must have policies preventing personnel from trading on advance knowledge of firm research actions.
regulatoryBasis: Investment Advisers Act Section 206; NASAA prohibited practices

stem: Under the Uniform Securities Act, the anti-fraud provisions apply to which persons in connection with the purchase or sale of a security?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only registered broker-dealers and investment advisers.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The anti-fraud provisions are not limited to registered persons. One of the most important principles of securities law is that anti-fraud rules apply universally — registration does not exempt a person, and lack of required registration does not exempt an unregistered person from fraud liability.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only persons who are required to register but have failed to do so.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Anti-fraud provisions apply to all persons — both those who are registered and those who are not. Unregistered persons face additional violations (failure to register), but that does not limit anti-fraud liability to them alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only issuers of securities, because they are in the best position to control disclosures.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Anti-fraud provisions apply far beyond issuers — they reach any person involved in securities transactions: advisers, broker-dealers, IARs, agents, and even unlicensed individuals who commit fraud in connection with securities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any person — registered or unregistered — in connection with the offer, sale, or purchase of any security.
choices.explanation: Correct. The Uniform Securities Act's anti-fraud provisions (Section 101) apply to 'any person' in connection with the offer, purchase, or sale of a security. Registration status is irrelevant to anti-fraud liability. Even exempt securities and exempt transactions are subject to the anti-fraud rules.

explanation: One of the foundational principles of the Uniform Securities Act and federal securities law (Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act) is that anti-fraud provisions apply universally — to any person in connection with any securities transaction. There are no registration-based safe harbors from fraud liability. An exemption from registration does not create an exemption from the anti-fraud rules, and neither does a securities or transaction exemption.
regulatoryBasis: Uniform Securities Act Section 101 (anti-fraud); Securities Exchange Act Section 10(b)

stem: An investment adviser's Form ADV Part 2B (the brochure supplement) primarily discloses information about which persons?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The advisory firm's disciplinary history and business practices.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Firm-level disciplinary history and business practices are disclosed in Form ADV Part 2A (the firm brochure), not Part 2B.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The identities and ownership interests of all shareholders holding more than 5% of the advisory firm.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Ownership information appears in Form ADV Part 1 (Schedule A and B), not in Part 2B. Part 2B focuses on individual supervised persons who directly advise clients.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The advisory firm's fee schedule, conflicts of interest, and investment strategies at the portfolio level.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Fees, conflicts, and portfolio-level investment strategies are disclosed in Form ADV Part 2A. Part 2B is specific to individual supervised persons who provide direct advice to clients.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The supervised persons (investment adviser representatives) who provide investment advice directly to clients.
choices.explanation: Correct. Form ADV Part 2B is the brochure supplement and must be delivered to clients for each supervised person who will provide investment advice to that client. It discloses the individual's educational background, business experience, disciplinary history, and other relationships. It supplements the firm-level disclosures in Part 2A.

explanation: Form ADV has three main parts: Part 1 (registration information, business description, ownership — filed electronically through IARD), Part 2A (the firm brochure — fees, conflicts, strategies, disciplinary history), and Part 2B (the brochure supplement — background on individual IARs/supervised persons who provide advice directly to clients). Part 2B must be delivered to each client for each supervised person providing direct advisory services to that client.
regulatoryBasis: Investment Advisers Act of 1940; SEC Rules 204-3 and Form ADV Instructions
